title: The Slaying of the Suitors (Mnēstērophonia)
greek: Μνηστηροφονία (Mnēstērophonia); ἆλτο δ' ἐπὶ μέγαν οὐδόν (alto d' epi megan oudon)
short: Odysseus throws off his beggar's rags and leaps to the great threshold of the hall: the disguise ends and the book traditionally titled 'the Slaying of the Suitors' begins.
body: Monro heads the book with its traditional Greek title, Mnēstērophonia. Odysseus takes his position on the 'great threshold' (megas oudos) at the entrance of the hall, the one way out; Monro notes that his aim is to stop the suitors escaping, while their only chance is to force him from the doorway and reach the town (22.76-8). His opening words take up Antinous' term for the contest, aaatos, 'decisive' (21.91): Antinous meant that it would settle the marriage, and it now proves decisive in a fatal sense. 'Another mark which no man has yet hit' is the suitors themselves, and his appeal to Apollo for glory (22.7) recalls the archer-god's festival (21.258).

title: The death of Antinous
greek: χρύσεον ἄμφωτον (chryseon amphōton)
short: Antinous, ringleader of the suitors, is shot through the throat just as he raises a golden cup to drink: 'death was not in his thoughts'.
body: The narrator dwells on the gap between the feast and the slaughter. The rhetorical question 'who would think...' (22.12-14) is usually taken to mean 'who would expect a single man among many to bring death on him?'; Monro argues that the pronoun hoi must be reflexive, so the sense is 'who would expect a man to bring death on himself' by attacking so many alone. The kick that spills the food, so that 'bread and roast flesh were befouled' (phoruneto, on an earthen floor, Monro), turns the suitors' endless banquet into filth. Antinous is the suitor who threw a footstool at the beggar (17.462-5) and who mocked the idea of the contest; he is the first to fall, as he had been 'the first to taste an arrow' in the narrator's forecast (21.98-100).

title: 'The cords of destruction had been made fast'
greek: ὀλέθρου πείρατ' ἐφῆπτο (olethrou peirat' ephēpto)
short: The suitors do not see that the ends of the rope of destruction have been fastened over them all: an image of inescapable doom that Odysseus then repeats.
body: Peirar (plural peirata) means a rope-end or the limit of something, and so 'completion, consummation'. Monro, comparing Il. 7.402 and 12.79, sees a play between the literal sense (the end of a rope, as of a net or snare) and the figurative sense (the final end of destruction). The narrator's comment at 22.33 is picked up in Odysseus' own speech at 22.41, so that what the narrator states, the hero declares. The image of a rope or net prepares the end of the book, when the disloyal maids die in a noose of ship's cable (22.465-73), and the simile of the suitors heaped like fish drawn in a net (22.383-9).

title: 'You dogs': Odysseus' indictment of the suitors
greek: ὦ κύνες (ō kunes); νέμεσις (nemesis)
short: Revealing himself, Odysseus names the suitors' three crimes: wasting his house, forcing the maids, and wooing his wife while he lived, fearing neither gods nor men's indignation.
body: Kuōn, 'dog', is the harshest Homeric term of abuse, implying shamelessness (compare Akhilleus' taunt that Agamemnon has 'the eyes of a dog', Il. 1.225). The speech is a formal accusation. The verb hupemnaasthe, 'you wooed covertly', implies, Monro notes, a wooing that went on alongside and therefore in conflict with the husband's rights. The suitors feared neither 'the gods who hold broad heaven' nor 'any nemesis of men to come hereafter': nemesis here is the righteous indignation of other people, the social sanction of shame, which Monro construes with deisantes, 'fearing'. The mention of the maids prepares the judgement on them at the end of the book. Eurymachus at once tries to put all the blame on the dead Antinous (22.45-59).

title: Compensation refused: 'the worth of twenty oxen'
greek: τιμὴν ἀμφὶς ἄγοντες ἐεικοσάβοιον (timēn amphis agontes eeikosaboion)
short: Eurymachus offers that each suitor will pay restitution worth twenty oxen in bronze and gold; Odysseus refuses all payment and demands full requital in blood.
body: Homeric society recognised settlement by payment: Ajax reminds Akhilleus that a man accepts blood-price (poinē) even from the killer of his brother or child (Il. 9.632-6). Wealth was reckoned in cattle; Laertes paid the worth of twenty oxen for Eurycleia (1.431). Eurymachus proposes a levy 'throughout the land' (kata dēmon, a contribution from the community, as Monro explains, cf. 13.14-15) to repay what has been eaten and drunk. The offer treats the wrong as an economic loss to be made good. Odysseus' answer, that not even all their fathers' wealth would stay his hands until they have paid for their transgression (huperbasiē), turns the matter from damages to punishment, and it is this refusal that creates the blood-feud resolved only at the end of Book XXIV.

title: The death of Amphinomus, the well-meaning suitor
greek: Ἀμφίνομος (Amphinomos)
short: Amphinomus, the most decent of the suitors, whom Odysseus had warned to leave, rushes at him and is killed by Telemachus' spear.
body: In Book XVIII Odysseus, moved by Amphinomus' kindness, gave him a solemn warning to go home before the master returned; Amphinomus went away 'shaking his head, for his heart foresaw evil', but stayed, 'for Athena had bound him to be slain by Telemachus' spear' (18.125-56). His death here fulfils that line exactly. The episode is central to the poem's moral design: the suitors are not all equally wicked, but staying in the house after being warned makes them all guilty. Monro discusses the verb eeisato, 'went at', 'made for' (22.89), and the danger Telemachus feared in drawing out his spear (22.97-8), which explains why he leaves it fixed and runs to bring armour.

title: The postern door (orsothurē) and the palace plan
greek: ὀρσοθύρη (orsothurē); λαύρη (laurē, passage); ῥῶγες μεγάροιο (rhōges megaroio)
short: A raised side door leads to a passage, and Melanthius finds a way to the store-room to arm the suitors: the most debated architecture in Homer.
body: Monro explains orsothurē as 'a raised door', probably a door or window above floor level, and laurē as one of the narrow passages of a house made up of several buildings. The phrase translated 'along the topmost level of the threshold' has never been satisfactorily explained. Melanthius objects that the court gate is 'terribly near' and the mouth of the passage narrow, so one man could block it; but he then climbs 'by the steps of the hall' (ana rhōgas megaroio) to the store-room. Of rhōges Monro writes that 'nothing can be said to be known', and suggests a flight of steps. The scene is a test case for reconstructions of the Homeric house, which Monro treats in a separate appendix; the narrative need is clear even when the plan is not.

anchor: hoist him up the tall pillar
title: The punishment of Melanthius the goatherd
greek: κίον' ἀν' ὑψηλὴν ἐρύσαι (kion' an' hupsēlēn erusai); σανίδας ἐκδῆσαι ὄπισθε (sanidas ekdēsai opisthe)
short: The treacherous goatherd is bound to boards, hoisted up a pillar to suffer through the battle, and afterwards mutilated and killed.
body: Melanthius, who kicked the disguised Odysseus (17.233-4) and supplied the suitors with arms, is caught in the store-room by Eumaeus and Philoetius. His hands and feet are bent back and lashed, and he is tied to boards and hauled up a column. Monro, following Döderlein, calls this 'a form of crucifixion', comparing the Athenians' treatment of the Persian Artayctes, 'nailed to boards and hanged' (Herodotus 9.120); in Homer the victim is bound, not nailed. Eumaeus' mockery about a soft bed and an early dawn (22.195-9) is, Monro says, a sustained piece of irony. At the end of the book his nose and ears are cut off, his genitals torn out for the dogs, and his hands and feet cut off (22.474-7): the very mutilation Antinous threatened in the Eurytion story (21.300-1) and the cruelty of 'king Echetus' (18.85-7).

title: Laertes' old shield
greek: σάκος εὐρὺ γέρον (sakos euru geron)
short: Melanthius is caught carrying out a broad old shield flecked with rust, the shield Laertes bore in his youth, its straps rotted: a glimpse of the family's past.
body: Monro notes that geron, 'old', is here applied to a thing, the only such use, and that kourizōn means 'when he was a young warrior' (kouros). The rotting straps show how long the house has been without fighting men. The detail prepares the final book, where the aged Laertes is restored by Athena, recalls his capture of Nericus 'when I was lord of the Cephallenians' (24.376-82), arms again 'a warrior perforce' (24.498-9) and kills Eupeithes with a spear-cast (24.516-25). The three generations of Laertes, Odysseus and Telemachus, each given a role in the defence of the house, are one of the unifying ideas of the end of the poem.

title: Athena as 'Mentor, son of Alcimus'
greek: Μέντωρ Ἀλκιμίδης (Mentōr Alkimidēs); ἑτεραλκὴς νίκη (heteralkēs nikē)
short: Athena appears in the form of Odysseus' old friend Mentor, rebukes him into fighting, and does not yet give full victory, but tests the courage of father and son.
body: Mentor, the Ithacan to whom Odysseus entrusted his household (2.225-7), is the shape Athena takes repeatedly to guide Telemachus (Books II-IV); she takes it again here and at the very end (24.502-48). Monro notes that the patronymic Alkimidēs, 'son of Alcimus', is 'a name chosen with a view to the context', since alkimos means 'valiant' and she is about to speak of alkē, 'strength in battle'. Her taunt contrasts Odysseus' nine years at Troy with his hesitation now. The phrase heteralkea nikēn (22.236), taken from the Iliad, means in Monro's explanation 'victory by other strength', that is, by the help of a new ally; Athena withholds it to test them. The modern word 'mentor' comes from this figure through Fénelon's novel Les Aventures de Télémaque (1699), where Mentor is Telemachus' wise guide.

anchor: in the guise of a swallow
title: Athena on the roof-beam 'like a swallow'
greek: χελιδόνι εἰκέλη ἄντην (chelidoni eikelē antēn)
short: Athena darts up to the smoke-blackened roof-beam and sits there 'like a swallow to look upon', watching the fight.
body: Whether Homer's gods actually turn into birds or are merely compared to them is an old question. At 1.320 Athena departs 'like a bird' (ornis d' hōs), and at 3.371-2 'in the likeness of a vulture', and readers disagree on each. Monro argues that antēn, 'face to face', strengthens eikelē so that she was 'like a swallow if set opposite to one', which 'seems to imply that Athene now took the shape of a swallow', not merely that she flew up like one. The image links back to the bowstring that sang 'like a swallow' (21.411). The goddess becomes a spectator, and the suitors, with their leader Agelaus, now believe that 'Mentor' has abandoned Odysseus (22.249-50).

title: Ctesippus' 'guest-gift' repaid
greek: τοῦτό τοι ἀντὶ ποδὸς ξεινήϊον (touto toi anti podos xeinēion)
short: The cowherd kills Ctesippus and taunts him: this spear is your guest-gift in return for the ox-hoof you 'gave' the beggar.
body: A xeinēion was the gift a host gave a departing guest, a central institution of hospitality. At 20.296-302 Ctesippus, a rich suitor from Same, announced that he would give the stranger a 'guest-gift' and hurled an ox-hoof at him. Philoetius now returns the joke in kind. The pattern of sarcastic 'guest-gifts' runs through the poem: the Cyclops promised Odysseus as his xeinēion that he would eat him last (9.369-70). Such inversions measure the suitors' crime, which is above all a violation of xenia, the reciprocal duties of host and guest. Ctesippus' father is named Polytherses (22.287), a name containing thersos, an older form of tharsos, 'boldness', which may hint at the son's insolence.

title: Athena raises the man-destroying aegis
greek: φθισίμβροτον αἰγίδ' ἀνέσχεν (phthisimbroton aigid' aneschen)
short: From the roof Athena holds up the aegis, 'bane of mortals', and the suitors' minds are struck with panic: the decisive divine intervention of the battle.
body: The aegis is the divine goatskin (aix, 'goat') or shield-like cape of Zeus, borne also by Athena and Apollo; in the Iliad it is fringed with tassels and carries the Gorgon's head, Terror and Rout (Il. 5.738-42), and Apollo shakes it to throw the Achaeans into panic (Il. 15.229-30, 15.318-22). Here alone in the Odyssey it is called phthisimbrotos, 'destroying mortals'. Monro notes that this interference, foreshadowed at 16.260 and earlier in this book (22.236), now begins, and that the terror-striking aegis was a chief attribute of the goddess in her own form. The effect is psychological, not physical: the suitors' wits are scattered (eptoiēthen), and the two similes that follow describe their rout.

title: Simile: cattle stampeded by the gadfly
greek: αἰόλος οἶστρος (aiolos oistros)
short: The panicking suitors flee through the hall like a herd of cattle maddened by a darting gadfly in spring, when the days grow long.
body: The oistros is the gadfly or breeze-fly whose bite drives cattle wild; from this physical sense the word later came to mean 'sting, frenzy, mad passion'. Monro glosses aiolos as 'darting, dancing about' and edonēsen as 'swept along', a verb used especially of the wind. The image reduces the suitors, who have spent years slaughtering Odysseus' cattle for their feasts, to cattle themselves. The seasonal note 'in spring, when the long days come' may reflect the time of the poem's action. The next simile, of vultures falling on smaller birds (22.302-8), changes viewpoint from the victims to the attackers, so that the pair shows the same moment from both sides.

title: Simile: vultures falling on small birds
greek: αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες ἀγκυλοχεῖλαι (aigupioi gampsōnyches ankylocheilai)
short: Odysseus and his three companions strike like vultures from the mountains on birds that cower low over the plain with no escape.
body: Monro explains nephea ptōssousai as 'shrinking from the region of the clouds', that is, flying as low as possible to escape. The comment 'and men rejoice at the chase' places a human audience inside the simile, as if the slaughter were a spectacle. The same birds of prey appear in the reunion of father and son, who weep 'more shrilly than birds, sea-eagles or crook-taloned vultures whose young the countrymen have taken' (16.216-18), so the image of the vulture links the recognition to the revenge. Monro notes that 22.308-9, the groaning as heads are struck and the floor swimming with blood, repeat Il. 10.483-4 and 21.20-1, with 'heads smitten' replacing 'struck by the sword'; the lines are repeated again by the dead Amphimedon (24.184-5).

anchor: By thy knees I beseech thee
title: Supplication refused: Leiodes at Odysseus' knees
greek: γουνοῦμαί σ', Ὀδυσεῦ· σὺ δέ μ' αἴδεο καί μ' ἐλέησον (gounoumai s', Odyseu: su de m' aideo kai m' eleēson)
short: Leiodes clasps Odysseus' knees in the ritual gesture of supplication, pleading innocence, but Odysseus beheads him.
body: Supplication (hiketeia) was a ritual act: the suppliant grasped the knees or chin of the one supplicated, asked for respect (aidōs) and pity, and, if accepted, came under the protection of Zeus Hikesios. John Gould's classic study showed how the physical contact made refusal a serious matter. Refusal is nonetheless possible in Homer: Agamemnon kills Adrastus (Il. 6.45-65) and Akhilleus kills Lycaon (Il. 21.64-119). Odysseus answers that as the suitors' seer Leiodes must often have prayed that Odysseus should not return, and Monro notes the irony of his reasoning ('you are likely to have prayed'), and that 'far from me' is a litotes for 'never'. The soothsayer's head is 'mingled with the dust while he was still speaking'. Two others who supplicate in this book, the bard and the herald, are spared.

title: Zeus Herkeios, god of the courtyard
greek: Διὸς μεγάλου ποτὶ βωμὸν ἑρκείου (Dios megalou poti bōmon herkeiou)
short: Phemius considers taking refuge at the altar of Zeus Herkeios in the courtyard, the household altar where Laertes and Odysseus had burned many offerings.
body: Herkeios comes from herkos, the fence or wall enclosing the courtyard (aulē), so Zeus Herkeios is Zeus as protector of the household enclosure. His altar stood in the court of a Greek house; in the Iliad Peleus sacrifices to Zeus 'in the enclosure of the court' (Il. 11.772-4). An altar was a place of asylum, and a suppliant seated at it claimed the god's protection. The most famous violation came at the sack of Troy: in the Epic Cycle's version Neoptolemus kills Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios (Apollodorus, Epitome 5.21), and he was himself later killed at Delphi. Phemius chooses instead to supplicate Odysseus directly; Monro discusses where the postern door must be for him to reach it. Medon and Phemius do later sit at this altar to await their fate (22.375-80).

title: Phemius son of Terpes, the bard
greek: Τερπιάδης... Φήμιος (Terpiadēs... Phēmios)
short: The suitors' singer Phemius has a 'speaking' name and patronymic: roughly 'Fame', son of 'Delight', the two things a bard gives.
body: Phēmios is related to phēmē, 'utterance, report, fame', and Terpiadēs, 'son of Terpes', to terpō, 'to delight', the regular verb for the pleasure of song (as when the suitors 'took delight' in Phemius' singing, 1.325-6, 347). Such significant names are common among Homer's minor characters (compare the Phaeacian names in Book VIII). Phemius sang for the suitors 'under compulsion' (anankēi), as the narrator says here and at 1.154, and his song of the Achaeans' bitter homecoming drew Penelope down in tears at 1.325-44. That he survives the massacre, spared at Telemachus' request, and is called on to play for the sham wedding (23.133-6) shows the poem's high valuation of the singer's art, which is also its own.

title: 'Self-taught am I': the bard's claim
greek: αὐτοδίδακτος δ' εἰμί, θεὸς δέ μοι ἐν φρεσὶν οἴμας παντοίας ἐνέφυσεν (autodidaktos d' eimi, theos de moi en phresin oimas pantoias enephusen)
short: Pleading for his life, Phemius claims to be 'self-taught', with all kinds of songs planted in his mind by a god: a famous statement about poetry.
body: The two halves seem to clash: how can a singer be self-taught and god-inspired? Most readers take autodidaktos to mean that no human master trained him, so that his art comes directly from the god. Monro suggests the word implies that the bard's craft 'was becoming, or had become, a regular profession, in which teaching might take the place of inspiration', so that Phemius is distinguishing himself from the trained craftsman. Oimai are 'lays' or 'paths' of song (compare oimē at 8.74 for Demodocus' song). Demodocus too is taught by the Muse (8.44-5, 8.479-81, 8.488). Phemius' argument is that killing a singer brings sorrow on the killer, since he sings 'to gods and men'; Monro takes eoika de toi paraeidein as 'I am fit to sing before you' as before a god.

title: Simile: the dead suitors like fish in a net
greek: ὥστ' ἰχθύας, οὕς θ' ἁλιῆες κοῖλον ἐς αἰγιαλὸν... δικτύῳ ἐξέρυσαν (hōst' ichthuas, hous th' halieēs koilon es aigialon... diktuōi exerusan)
short: Odysseus finds the suitors heaped like fish dragged in a net onto a curving beach, longing for the sea while the sun takes their life.
body: Monro explains koilon, 'hollow', as 'curving': the fishermen draw their nets into a bay. The simile is unusually long and pathetic for a scene of punishment: the fish 'long for the waves of the sea' (pothēonta kumata) as the sun dries them. It echoes the net image of the 'cords of destruction' (22.33, 41), and recalls the Scylla episode, where Odysseus' companions are lifted like fish on a line and he calls the sight 'the most pitiful' of his wanderings (12.251-9). The viewpoint is Odysseus' own as he surveys the hall, so the simile hints at what he sees as well as what he has done.

title: Simile: Odysseus bloodied like a lion
greek: αἵματι καὶ λύθρῳ πεπαλαγμένον ὥστε λέοντα (haimati kai luthrōi pepalagmenon hōste leonta)
short: Eurycleia finds Odysseus spattered with blood and filth like a lion that has fed on a farm ox, terrible to look upon.
body: Lion similes run through Odysseus' story. Menelaus predicted that Odysseus would return like a lion to a deer's lair where she had laid her fawns (4.333-40, repeated by Telemachus at 17.124-31), and the naked, brine-crusted Odysseus approached Nausicaa's maids 'like a mountain lion' (6.130-6). Here the prophecy is fulfilled, and the image is frankly frightening: the 'ox of the farmstead' (bous agraulos) recalls the suitors' feasting on the master's cattle. Monro notes that the line describing the corpses and blood reappears in the manuscripts at 23.48, where it is 'clearly out of place'. The simile gives Eurycleia's view and leads straight to her cry of triumph.

title: The ololygē, the women's ritual cry
greek: ἴθυσέν ῥ' ὀλολύξαι (ithusen rh' ololuxai)
short: Seeing the dead, Eurycleia starts to raise the ololygē, the shrill cry Greek women uttered at the climax of a sacrifice; Odysseus checks her.
body: Monro explains the ololygē as a joyful cry uttered by women, 'especially at the moment of the consummation of a sacrifice', as when the women cry out as the ox is struck at Nestor's sacrifice (3.450); Penelope also cries it in prayer (4.767). Herodotus thought the ritual cry originated with the women of Libya, who were excellent at it (4.189). Monro's note even records women at Zakopane, in what he calls Austrian Poland, crying out when the wafer is lifted at Mass, as a possible survival. Eurycleia's impulse treats the slaughter as a completed sacrifice, an idea that fits the many sacrificial overtones of the scene (the festival of Apollo, the 'supper', the purification that follows). Odysseus forbids it, for reasons he states at once.

title: 'It is not holy to exult over slain men'
greek: οὐχ ὁσίη κταμένοισιν ἐπ' ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι (ouch hosiē ktamenoisin ep' andrasin euchetaasthai)
short: Odysseus tells Eurycleia to rejoice in silence: it is unholy to boast over the dead, for the gods' fate and the suitors' own reckless acts destroyed them.
body: Hosiē means what is permitted or right in the eyes of the gods. The rule is striking after the Iliad, where warriors regularly vaunt over fallen enemies (Akhilleus over Hector, Il. 22.331-6). Monro's additional notes compare a line of Archilochus, that it is not noble to jeer at dead men (fr. 64 Bergk). Odysseus presents himself as the agent of divine justice rather than a personal avenger: the suitors were overcome by 'the fate of the gods' (moira theōn) and their own 'reckless deeds' (schetlia erga). Monro comments on 'neither evil nor good' (22.415): the point is that they honoured good men no more than bad, that is, not at all. The same verdict is repeated by Penelope at 23.65-7.

title: The hanging of the twelve maids
greek: μὴ μὲν δὴ καθαρῷ θανάτῳ (mē men dē katharōi thanatōi); κίχλαι τανυσίπτεροι (kichlai tanusipteroi)
short: Telemachus refuses the disloyal maids a 'clean death' by the sword and hangs them from a ship's cable, their deaths compared to thrushes or doves caught in a snare.
body: Eurycleia names twelve of the fifty women as having 'walked in shamelessness' (22.424). Odysseus orders them killed with swords between the round building called the tholos and the courtyard fence; Monro admits that the nature and purpose of this 'dome-shaped building' are unknown. Telemachus instead chooses hanging, refusing them a katharos thanatos, a clean (unpolluted or honourable) death. The simile, of birds caught in a net set in a thicket when they seek their roost, 'and hateful is the bed that receives them', contains what Monro calls an oxymoron: the stugeros koitos, 'hateful bed', recalls the beds the women shared with the suitors. 'They writhed a little with their feet, but not long' is one of the starkest lines in Homer. The passage has troubled many modern readers; Margaret Atwood's novel The Penelopiad (2005) retells the story from the maids' viewpoint.

title: Purification with sulphur and fire
greek: οἶσε θέειον, γρηΰ, κακῶν ἄκος (oise theeion, grēu, kakōn akos); θεειώσω (theeiōsō)
short: Odysseus calls for sulphur, 'the cure of ills', and fire, and fumigates the hall, house and courtyard to cleanse them of the pollution of killing.
body: Bloodshed brought miasma, ritual pollution, which had to be removed before normal life and worship could resume. Burning sulphur (theeion) was the traditional purifier: in the Iliad Akhilleus cleans a sacred cup with sulphur before praying to Zeus (Il. 16.228). Monro discusses the unusual form thēion in the manuscripts and the odd phrase 'hall and house and court', suggesting the original may have been the conventional 'chamber and house and court' for the whole palace. Only after purification does Odysseus allow the loyal women to come and greet him (22.495-501), and in Book XXIII Eurycleia tells Penelope that he is purging the house with sulphur (23.50-1). The ritual marks the transition from slaughter back to household order.
